shared.concept_anchor: State ratification threshold under Article 368

en.display_text:
Regarding state ratification under the constitutional amendment procedure, which one of the following statements is correct?

(a) Ratification must be completed within six months by the required number of states
(b) All state legislatures must ratify the amendment for it to be valid
(c) Ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the states is required, and no time limit is prescribed
(d) All state legislative assemblies must ratify, though legislative councils may be bypassed
en.strong_distractor: d — Option d is deceptive because the word 'all' sounds constitutionally authoritative, and students often reason that state sovereignty demands unanimous consent for federal changes.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): there is no time limit prescribed under Article 368 for state ratification — the Constitution is silent on this.
Eliminate option (b): ratification by all states is not required; Article 368 requires only a majority of state legislatures, not unanimity.
Eliminate option (d): 'all states' is an overstatement; the correct threshold is more than half (50%) of the total states.
Confirm option (c): Article 368 specifies ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the states, with no time limit attached.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently conflate the state ratification requirement with unanimity, reasoning by analogy with federal systems like the USA where supermajority of states is required. The Indian Constitution requires ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the states — a simple numerical majority of states, not all of them. Additionally, the Constitution prescribes no time limit within which states must ratify, a detail that trips candidates who assume Parliament can set a deadline.
en.final_explanation:
Article 368 establishes a three-tier amendment procedure. The most stringent tier requires a special majority in Parliament AND ratification by legislatures of not less than one-half of the total states. This applies to provisions touching federalism — such as election of the President, extent of executive power of Union and States, and representation in Rajya Sabha.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: No time limit for ratification exists under Article 368. States can ratify at any time without constitutional compulsion of a deadline.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 'All states' is never required. The threshold is at least half of all states.
• Option (c) — Correct: More than half of states must ratify, and no time limit is prescribed — this is the precise constitutional requirement.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Same error as (b); universality is not the standard.

Value Addition:
• Ratification must come from state legislatures, not state governments or governors.
• The President cannot withhold assent to a constitutional amendment bill — made mandatory by the 24th Amendment.
• Only about 8–10 categories of provisions require state ratification.

संवैधानिक संशोधन प्रक्रिया के अंतर्गत राज्य अनुमोदन के संबंध में निम्नलिखित में से कौन-सा कथन सही है?

(a) आवश्यक राज्यों की संख्या द्वारा अनुमोदन छह महीने के भीतर पूरा होना चाहिए
(b) संशोधन को मान्य करने के लिए सभी राज्य विधानसभाओं का अनुमोदन आवश्यक है
(c) कम से कम आधे राज्यों की विधानसभाओं द्वारा अनुमोदन आवश्यक है, और कोई समय सीमा निर्धारित नहीं है
(d) सभी राज्य विधानसभाओं को अनुमोदन करना चाहिए, हालांकि विधान परिषदों को छोड़ा जा सकता है
hi.strong_distractor: d — विकल्प d भ्रामक है क्योंकि 'सभी' शब्द संवैधानिक रूप से अधिकारप्रदर्शक लगता है, और छात्र अक्सर यह तर्क करते हैं कि राज्य संप्रभुता के कारण संघीय परिवर्तनों के लिए सर्वसम्मति आवश्यक है।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (a) को हटाएं: अनुच्छेद 368 के अंतर्गत राज्य अनुमोदन के लिए कोई समय सीमा निर्धारित नहीं है — संविधान इस विषय में मौन है।
विकल्प (b) को हटाएं: सभी राज्यों द्वारा अनुमोदन आवश्यक नहीं है; अनुच्छेद 368 केवल अधिकांश राज्यों की विधानसभाओं द्वारा अनुमोदन की मांग करता है, सर्वसम्मति नहीं।
विकल्प (d) को हटाएं: 'सभी राज्य' एक अतिशयोक्ति है; सही सीमा कुल राज्यों के आधे से अधिक (50%) है।
विकल्प (c) की पुष्टि करें: अनुच्छेद 368 में राज्यों की विधानसभाओं द्वारा कम से कम आधे से अधिक राज्यों के अनुमोदन का प्रावधान है, और कोई समय सीमा नहीं है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: छात्र अक्सर राज्य अनुमोदन की आवश्यकता को सर्वसम्मति से भ्रमित कर देते हैं, और अमेरिकी जैसे संघीय प्रणालियों के साथ तुलना करते हैं जहाँ राज्यों की सुपरमेज़ोरिटी आवश्यक होती है। भारतीय संविधान में राज्यों की विधानसभाओं द्वारा कम से कम आधे से अधिक राज्यों के अनुमोदन की आवश्यकता है — सभी राज्यों की नहीं। इसके अतिरिक्त, संविधान में राज्यों को अनुमोदन के लिए कोई समय सीमा निर्धारित नहीं है, जो उन उम्मीदवारों के लिए भ्रम पैदा करता है जो मानते हैं कि संसद समय सीमा निर्धारित कर सकती है।
hi.final_explanation:
अनुच्छेद 368 तीन-स्तरीय संशोधन प्रक्रिया स्थापित करता है। सबसे कठोर स्तर में संसद में विशेष बहुमत और कुल राज्यों की कम से कम आधी से अधिक विधानसभाओं द्वारा अनुमोदन आवश्यक है। यह संघीयता से संबंधित प्रावधानों पर लागू होता है — जैसे राष्ट्रपति का चुनाव, केंद्र और राज्यों के कार्यकारी शक्तियों की सीमा, और राज्यसभा में प्रतिनिधित्व।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: अनुच्छेद 368 के अंतर्गत अनुमोदन के लिए कोई समय सीमा नहीं है। राज्य किसी भी समय बिना संवैधानिक बाध्यता के अनुमोदन कर सकते हैं।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: 'सभी राज्य' कभी आवश्यक नहीं है। सीमा कम से कम आधे राज्यों की है।
• विकल्प (c) — सही: आधे से अधिक राज्यों का अनुमोदन आवश्यक है, और कोई समय सीमा निर्धारित नहीं है — यह संवैधानिक आवश्यकता है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: (b) जैसा ही त्रुटि; सार्वभौमिकता मानक नहीं है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• अनुमोदन राज्य सरकारों या राज्यपालों से नहीं, बल्कि राज्य विधानसभाओं से आना चाहिए।
• राष्ट्रपति संवैधानिक संशोधन विधेयक को स्वीकृति देने से इनकार नहीं कर सकते — यह 24वें संशोधन द्वारा अनिवार्य किया गया है।
• केवल लगभग 8–10 प्रकार के प्रावधानों के लिए राज्य अनुमोदन आवश्यक होता है।

shared.concept_anchor: First Amendment 1951 — Ninth Schedule genesis

en.display_text:
With reference to the First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951, consider the following statements:

1. It inserted the Ninth Schedule to place certain laws beyond challenge on grounds of Fundamental Rights.
2. It was enacted in response to the Supreme Court's ruling in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras.
3. It expanded the permissible grounds for the State to impose reasonable restrictions on the right to free speech.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 2 only
(b) 1 and 3 only
(c) 2 and 3 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 inserted the Ninth Schedule to place certain laws beyond challenge on grounds of Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The Ninth Schedule was added by the First Amendment precisely to shield land reform legislation from being struck down under Articles 14, 19, and 31.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 was enacted to override the Supreme Court's ruling in A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras.
statement_analysis.reason: The First Amendment responded to the judgment in State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan. Gopalan dealt with preventive detention, not property rights or educational reservations.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Constitutional Amendment expanded the grounds on which the State could impose reasonable restrictions on the right to free speech under Article 19.
statement_analysis.reason: The Amendment inserted 'reasonable restrictions' language in Articles 19(2) and 19(4), broadening the grounds — including public order and relations with foreign states — on which free speech could be curtailed.

en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who recall the Ninth Schedule correctly may also conflate the Champakam Dorairajan case with A.K. Gopalan, both of which were landmark early 1950s Supreme Court decisions.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The Ninth Schedule was indeed added by the First Amendment to protect land reform laws from Fundamental Rights challenges — this is accurate.
Eliminate Statement 2 as incorrect: The relevant Supreme Court case was Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan — entity-swap trap; any option pairing Statement 2 as correct must be eliminated.
Confirm Statement 3: Expanded restrictions on Article 19 rights were a direct feature of the First Amendment — correct.
The only option with Statements 1 and 3 correct and Statement 2 incorrect is option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras (1950) is a famous early Supreme Court case about personal liberty under Article 21, not about property rights or educational reservations. The First Amendment was Parliament's direct response to State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, which invalidated communal reservation in educational institutions. A candidate who has memorised both landmark cases but not their specific triggers will easily confuse them here.
en.final_explanation:
The First Constitutional Amendment (1951) was Parliament's earliest assertion of its authority over judicial interpretations of Fundamental Rights. It responded directly to Champakam Dorairajan, where the Supreme Court struck down caste-based reservation in admissions to state colleges.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Ninth Schedule was created by this amendment to insulate land reform laws from judicial review under Part III.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The triggering case was Champakam Dorairajan, not A.K. Gopalan. Gopalan concerned preventive detention and Article 21.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Articles 19(2) and 19(4) were amended to add broader grounds for restricting free speech, including public order and incitement to offences.

Value Addition:
• The First Amendment is historically significant as the first instance of Parliament overriding a Supreme Court judgment through a constitutional amendment.
• The Ninth Schedule originally contained only 13 laws; it grew to 284 laws over decades.
• The First Amendment is also the genesis of the Parliament–Judiciary conflict over constitutional supremacy.

shared.concept_anchor: Basic Structure — cases and elements

table_data.header_text: Match the Supreme Court cases in List I with the Basic Structure elements or constitutional principles primarily associated with them in List II:
rows: A. Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
1. Free and fair elections as a Basic Structure element
B. Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
2. Supremacy of the Constitution and republican democratic form
C. Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
3. Harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
D. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)
4. Speaker's orders under Tenth Schedule subject to judicial review
table_data.footer_text:
Which of the following is the correct matching?

(a) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(b) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(c) A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4
(d) A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4

en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students may correctly pair free and fair elections with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain but then misremember that Kesavananda itself mentioned the separation of powers explicitly.
elimination_logic: Free and fair elections as a Basic Structure element was identified in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), not Kesavananda — this eliminates options where A is matched to 1.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) is correctly matched with supremacy of the Constitution and republican democratic form — List II item 2 is the correct match for A.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) dealt with the Tenth Schedule and Speaker's authority, not Basic Structure elements per se — match D to 4.
Minerva Mills (1980) added harmony between FR and DPSPs — match C to 3. Confirm: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 = option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in attributing Basic Structure elements to the wrong case. 'Free and fair elections' is often remembered as a Kesavananda contribution because students associate all Basic Structure articulation with that landmark. However, Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) was the case that specifically added free and fair elections to the Basic Structure. Kesavananda focused on the foundational elements: supremacy of Constitution, democratic republican form, and secular character.
en.final_explanation:
The Basic Structure doctrine evolved through multiple Supreme Court judgments, with each case adding new elements or reinforcing existing ones. Matching each element to its correct originating case tests precision of knowledge.

• A (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973): The foundational case identified supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, and federalism — matched to List II item 2.
• B (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975): Free and fair elections was identified as a Basic Structure element in this case arising from the Allahabad HC judgment on Indira Gandhi's election — matched to List II item 1.
• C (Minerva Mills, 1980): Harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSPs was declared a Basic Structure element, and limited amending power was reinforced — matched to List II item 3.
• D (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992): The Speaker's authority under the Tenth Schedule was upheld but subjected to judicial review — matched to item 4.

Value Addition:
• The Basic Structure doctrine has no exhaustive codified list in the Constitution — it is entirely judge-made.
• Each major amendment from 1971–1985 was a parliamentary attempt to push back against judicial expansion of Basic Structure.
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) added federalism as an independently enforceable Basic Structure element.

elimination_logic: मूल संरचना तत्व के रूप में स्वतंत्र और निष्पक्ष चुनाव Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) में पहचाना गया था, न कि Kesavananda में — इससे वे विकल्प समाप्त हो जाते हैं जहाँ A को 1 से जोड़ा गया है।
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) को संविधान की सर्वोच्चता और गणतांत्रिक लोकतांत्रिक रूप के साथ सही ढंग से जोड़ा गया है — सूची II का आइटम 2 A के लिए सही मेल है।
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) ने दसवें अनुसूची और स्पीकर के अधिकार से संबंधित मामलों को संभाला, न कि सीधे मूल संरचना तत्वों को — D को 4 से मिलाएं।
Minerva Mills (1980) ने मौलिक अधिकारों और निर्देशात्मक सिद्धांतों के बीच सामंजस्य जोड़ा — C को 3 से मिलाएं। पुष्टि करें: A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4 = विकल्प (b)।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: फंदा इस बात में है कि मूल संरचना तत्वों को गलत मामले से जोड़ा जाए। 'स्वतंत्र और निष्पक्ष चुनाव' को अक्सर Kesavananda का योगदान समझा जाता है क्योंकि छात्र सभी मूल संरचना के तत्वों को उसी महत्वपूर्ण मामले से जोड़ते हैं। हालांकि, स्वतंत्र और निष्पक्ष चुनाव को मूल संरचना में विशेष रूप से Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) के मामले में जोड़ा गया था। Kesavananda ने संविधान की सर्वोच्चता, लोकतांत्रिक गणतांत्रिक रूप, और धर्मनिरपेक्ष चरित्र जैसे मूलभूत तत्वों पर ध्यान केंद्रित किया।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• मूल संरचना सिद्धांत का संविधान में कोई संपूर्ण सूचीबद्ध कोडित सूची नहीं है — यह पूरी तरह से न्यायाधीश निर्मित है।
• 1971–1985 के प्रत्येक प्रमुख संशोधन ने मूल संरचना के न्यायिक विस्तार के खिलाफ संसदीय प्रयास किया।
• S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) ने संघवाद को स्वतंत्र रूप से लागू होने वाले मूल संरचना तत्व के रूप में जोड़ा।

shared.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule — Speaker's authority and judicial review

en.display_text:
Rajan, a member of the Lok Sabha, voted against his party's official whip on a key piece of legislation. His party has filed a petition seeking his disqualification under the provisions of the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution. Rajan believes the petition is frivolous and wishes to challenge it. Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position in this scenario?

(a) The Speaker of the Lok Sabha will adjudicate the petition, and the Speaker's decision is absolute and cannot be challenged in any court of law
(b) The petition must be referred to the President, who will decide the matter after seeking the opinion of the Election Commission
(c) The Election Commission of India has exclusive jurisdiction over disqualification matters under the Tenth Schedule
(d) The Speaker of the Lok Sabha will adjudicate the petition, and the final order passed by the Speaker can be challenged before the High Court or the Supreme Court
en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because the President does play a role in constitutional matters, and students may confuse referral to the President with the Speaker's adjudicatory role under the Tenth Schedule.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Supreme Court in Kihoto Hollohan held that Speaker's orders under the Tenth Schedule are subject to judicial review — they are not final and unchallengeable.
Eliminate option (b): Defection cases are decided by the Speaker (Lok Sabha) or Chairman (Rajya Sabha) — not referred to the President for adjudication.
Eliminate option (c): The Election Commission has no jurisdiction over defection matters — its role is in elections, not post-election disqualification for defection.
Confirm option (d): The Speaker is the adjudicating authority; the order can be challenged in the High Court or Supreme Court after the Speaker decides — not before.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The scenario is designed to test whether students know that judicial review of Speaker's orders is available but only after the order is made, not as a prior check. Students who recall that 'Speaker's decision is final' from a shallow reading of the Tenth Schedule will incorrectly choose option (a). Kihoto Hollohan specifically clarified that while the Speaker has primacy, courts retain the power of judicial review of the final order.
en.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule (added by the 52nd Amendment, 1985) provides for disqualification of legislators on grounds of defection. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha (or Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) is designated as the sole adjudicating authority for defection petitions.

Applicable principle: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but held that the Speaker's orders are subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice — and only after the order is passed.

Scenario analysis: Rajan's petition must be submitted to the Speaker, who will adjudicate it. If dissatisfied, Rajan can challenge the Speaker's final order in the High Court or Supreme Court.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Speaker's orders are reviewable — they are not absolutely final.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The President is not the adjudicating authority under the Tenth Schedule.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Election Commission handles election-related matters, not defection disqualifications.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Speaker adjudicates; courts can review the order after it is passed.

Value Addition:
• The 91st Amendment (2003) raised the merger threshold from 1/3rd to 2/3rd of party members.
• Defection disqualification proceedings do not bar future election candidacy.
• Para 2 of the Tenth Schedule covers voluntary giving up of party membership and voting against party whip.

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements regarding the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988:

Statement 1: It amended Article 326 to lower the minimum voting age for elections to the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies from 21 to 18 years.
Statement 2: As a consequence of this amendment, the minimum age for contesting elections to the Lok Sabha was also reduced to 18 years.

Which of the following is correct?

(a) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct
(b) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are incorrect
(c) Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect
(d) Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct

statement_analysis.statement: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988 amended Article 326 to lower the minimum age for voting in elections to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies from 21 to 18 years.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 326 was amended by the 61st Amendment to reduce the voting age from 21 to 18 years for elections to both the House of the People and legislative assemblies of states.

statement_analysis.statement: As a consequence of the 61st Amendment, the minimum age for contesting elections to the Lok Sabha was also lowered to 18 years.
statement_analysis.reason: The 61st Amendment changed only the voting age (franchise), not the age of candidacy. The minimum age to contest Lok Sabha or state assembly elections remains 25 years, and for Rajya Sabha or state legislative councils, it remains 30 years.

en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 may assume that lowering the voting age logically implies a corresponding lowering of the candidacy age, making 'both correct' seem reasonable.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is verifiable and correct — Article 326 was amended by the 61st Amendment to reduce the voting age to 18.

Statement 2 conflates voting age (franchise) with candidacy age — these are governed by different provisions. Candidacy age for Lok Sabha is 25 years under Article 84, unchanged by the 61st Amendment.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect, the answer is option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: This is a classic conflation trap — voting age and candidacy age are distinct constitutional provisions. Voting eligibility is under Article 326; candidacy requirements are under Articles 84 (Parliament) and 173 (State Legislatures). The 61st Amendment touched only Article 326. A student who merges these two concepts will incorrectly believe both were changed, selecting option (a).
en.final_explanation:
The 61st Amendment (1988) was enacted to enfranchise India's large youth population by reducing the voting age from 21 to 18 years.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Article 326 was specifically amended; the 18-year voting age applies to both Lok Sabha and state assembly elections.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Candidacy age was not affected. Article 84 requires a candidate to be at least 25 years for Lok Sabha, and Article 173 requires the same for state assemblies. These remain unchanged.

Value Addition:
• The voting age for Rajya Sabha elections (indirect, through MLAs) is also 18 now since MLAs themselves were elected at 18+.
• Minimum age of candidacy: Lok Sabha/Vidhan Sabha = 25 years; Rajya Sabha/Vidhan Parishad = 30 years.
• This amendment required only a special majority — it does not fall under the state ratification category despite affecting elections.

shared.concept_anchor: Article 21A — age group 6–14 and exclusion of below-6

en.display_text:
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, provides for the right to free and compulsory education as a Fundamental Right for children in the age group of ________.

(a) 6 to 14 years
(b) 0 to 14 years
(c) 0 to 18 years
(d) 6 to 18 years
en.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who recall the '86th Amendment = RTE' may not remember the precise age bracket, and 0–14 sounds comprehensive and child-welfare oriented.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Article 21A covers children aged 6–14, not 0–14 — children below 6 are covered under Article 45 (DPSP), not as a Fundamental Right.
Eliminate option (c): The age range 0–18 was never part of Article 21A — it overstates the right significantly.
Eliminate option (d): 6–18 is also incorrect; 18 is the voting age, not the RTE boundary.
Confirm option (a): Article 21A specifies children aged 6 to 14 years — this is the precise constitutional text.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The exclusion of children below 6 from Article 21A is a high-frequency UPSC trap. The 86th Amendment simultaneously narrowed Article 45's DPSP to focus on early childhood care for below-6 children, while making education a Fundamental Right only for 6–14. A student who reads 'right to education' and assumes it covers all children from birth will select 0–14 or 0–18.
en.final_explanation:
The 86th Amendment (2002) operated on three constitutional provisions simultaneously. It inserted Article 21A, amended Article 45, and added a Fundamental Duty in Article 51A.

• Option (a) — Correct: Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education specifically for children between 6 and 14 years of age.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 0–14 is wrong. Children below 6 are covered under the amended Article 45 as a DPSP, not under Article 21A.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 0–18 vastly overstates the scope of Article 21A.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: 6–18 is also incorrect; the upper age limit is 14, not 18.

Value Addition:
• The Right to Education Act (2009) was enacted to operationalise Article 21A.
• Article 45 (after 86th Amendment) directs the State to provide early childhood care for children below 6 — it is a DPSP, not a FR.
• Parents/guardians have a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k) to provide educational opportunities to their children aged 6–14.

hi.display_text:
86वें संविधान संशोधन अधिनियम, 2002 द्वारा जोड़ा गया अनुच्छेद 21A, बच्चों के लिए ________ आयु वर्ग में मुफ्त और अनिवार्य शिक्षा का मौलिक अधिकार प्रदान करता है।

(a) 6 से 14 वर्ष
(b) 0 से 14 वर्ष
(c) 0 से 18 वर्ष
(d) 6 से 18 वर्ष
hi.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प (c) भ्रमित करने वाला है क्योंकि छात्र जो '86वां संशोधन = RTE' याद करते हैं, वे सटीक आयु सीमा याद नहीं रख पाते, और 0–14 व्यापक और बाल-कल्याण उन्मुख लगता है।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (b) को हटाएं: अनुच्छेद 21A 6–14 वर्ष के बच्चों को कवर करता है, 0–14 नहीं — 6 वर्ष से कम के बच्चे अनुच्छेद 45 (DPSP) के अंतर्गत आते हैं, मौलिक अधिकार के रूप में नहीं।
विकल्प (c) को हटाएं: 0–18 की आयु सीमा कभी अनुच्छेद 21A का हिस्सा नहीं थी — यह अधिकार को अत्यधिक बढ़ा-चढ़ाकर प्रस्तुत करता है।
विकल्प (d) को हटाएं: 6–18 भी गलत है; 18 मतदान की आयु है, RTE की सीमा नहीं।
विकल्प (a) की पुष्टि करें: अनुच्छेद 21A स्पष्ट रूप से 6 से 14 वर्ष के बच्चों के लिए है — यह संवैधानिक पाठ का सटीक विवरण है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: अनुच्छेद 21A से 6 वर्ष से कम के बच्चों को बाहर रखना UPSC में एक उच्च-आवृत्ति वाला जाल है। 86वां संशोधन अनुच्छेद 45 के DPSP को 6 वर्ष से कम के बच्चों के लिए प्रारंभिक बाल देखभाल पर केंद्रित करते हुए संकुचित करता है, जबकि शिक्षा को केवल 6–14 वर्ष के लिए मौलिक अधिकार बनाता है। जो छात्र 'शिक्षा का अधिकार' पढ़ते हैं और मान लेते हैं कि यह जन्म से सभी बच्चों को कवर करता है, वे 0–14 या 0–18 चुनेंगे।
hi.final_explanation:
86वां संशोधन (2002) ने तीन संवैधानिक प्रावधानों पर एक साथ कार्य किया। इसने अनुच्छेद 21A जोड़ा, अनुच्छेद 45 में संशोधन किया, और अनुच्छेद 51A में एक मौलिक कर्तव्य जोड़ा।

• विकल्प (a) — सही: अनुच्छेद 21A विशेष रूप से 6 से 14 वर्ष के बच्चों के लिए मुफ्त और अनिवार्य शिक्षा की गारंटी देता है।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: 0–14 गलत है। 6 वर्ष से कम के बच्चे संशोधित अनुच्छेद 45 के तहत DPSP के रूप में आते हैं, न कि अनुच्छेद 21A के तहत।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: 0–18 अनुच्छेद 21A के दायरे को अत्यधिक बढ़ा-चढ़ाकर प्रस्तुत करता है।
• विकल्प (d) — गलत: 6–18 भी गलत है; अधिकतम आयु सीमा 14 है, 18 नहीं।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• शिक्षा का अधिकार अधिनियम (2009) अनुच्छेद 21A को लागू करने के लिए बनाया गया था।
• अनुच्छेद 45 (86वें संशोधन के बाद) राज्य को 6 वर्ष से कम के बच्चों के लिए प्रारंभिक बाल देखभाल प्रदान करने का निर्देश देता है — यह DPSP है, मौलिक अधिकार नहीं।
• माता-पिता/अभिभावकों का अनुच्छेद 51A(k) के तहत 6–14 वर्ष के बच्चों को शैक्षिक अवसर प्रदान करना एक मौलिक कर्तव्य है।

concepts_used: 99th Amendment Act, 2014 and the NJAC Judgment (2015): Judicial Appointments Controversy

shared.concept_anchor: 99th Amendment NJAC struck down despite state ratification

en.display_text:
The Supreme Court's judgment in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) concerning the 99th Constitutional Amendment is constitutionally significant primarily because it demonstrated that:

(a) The Supreme Court upheld the National Judicial Appointments Commission as consistent with the doctrine of separation of powers
(b) A constitutional amendment ratified by the required number of state legislatures cannot be invalidated by the Supreme Court on any ground
(c) The inclusion of the Union Law Minister in a judicial appointments body violates the basic structure solely on the ground of conflict of interest
(d) Even a constitutionally valid amendment — enacted with proper majority and state ratification — can be struck down if it violates the Basic Structure of the Constitution
en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students may reason that proper procedural compliance (state ratification) should be an absolute shield — the idea that a validly enacted amendment can still be struck down for Basic Structure violation is counterintuitive.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Supreme Court did not uphold the NJAC — it was struck down; this option is factually false.
Eliminate option (b): State ratification was indeed completed, but the Court held this irrelevant to the Basic Structure question — correct procedure does not immunise against substantive invalidity.
Eliminate option (c): The Law Minister's inclusion was noted as problematic, but the precise holding was about 'primacy of judiciary' in appointments as a Basic Structure element.
Confirm option (d): The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment on the ground that the NJAC compromised judicial independence, which is part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The NJAC judgment illustrates that procedural compliance — including state ratification — does not protect a constitutional amendment from Basic Structure challenge. Many students incorrectly assume that if Parliament follows the correct amending procedure (special majority + state ratification), courts cannot invalidate the amendment. This question directly tests that misconception. The correct understanding is that procedural validity and substantive validity are independent requirements.
en.final_explanation:
The 99th Amendment (2014) replaced the Collegium system with the National Judicial Appointments Commission — a 6-member body comprising the Chief Justice of India, two senior judges, the Union Law Minister, and two 'eminent persons'.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Supreme Court did not uphold the NJAC — it was unanimously struck down in the 2015 judgment by a 4:1 majority.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The amendment had been ratified by more than half the states, satisfying procedural requirements. The Court held that correct procedure cannot save an amendment that violates Basic Structure.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: While the Law Minister's inclusion was a concern, the core holding was broader — judicial independence as a Basic Structure element was at stake.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Court held that the NJAC violated judicial independence, which is a component of the Basic Structure, and therefore struck down the amendment.

Value Addition:
• The case is: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015).
• 'Primacy of the judiciary' in judicial appointments was declared a Basic Structure element.
• The Collegium system (evolved through Three Judges Cases) was restored by this judgment.

hi.display_text:
सुप्रीम कोर्ट के निर्णय Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015) में 99वें संवैधानिक संशोधन के संबंध में संवैधानिक महत्व इस बात में है कि:

(a) सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने राष्ट्रीय न्यायिक नियुक्ति आयोग को शक्तियों के पृथक्करण के सिद्धांत के अनुरूप स्वीकार किया
(b) एक संवैधानिक संशोधन जिसे आवश्यक संख्या में राज्य विधानसभाओं ने स्वीकृत किया है, उसे सुप्रीम कोर्ट किसी भी आधार पर अमान्य नहीं कर सकता
(c) न्यायिक नियुक्ति निकाय में केंद्रीय कानून मंत्री का शामिल होना केवल हितों के टकराव के आधार पर मूल संरचना का उल्लंघन करता है
(d) एक संवैधानिक रूप से वैध संशोधन — जो उचित बहुमत और राज्य की स्वीकृति के साथ पारित किया गया हो — भी यदि मूल संरचना का उल्लंघन करता है तो उसे खारिज किया जा सकता है
hi.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प (b) भ्रामक है क्योंकि छात्र यह तर्क कर सकते हैं कि उचित प्रक्रिया का पालन (राज्य की स्वीकृति) एक पूर्ण सुरक्षा कवच होना चाहिए — यह विचार कि एक वैध रूप से पारित संशोधन को भी मूल संरचना के उल्लंघन के कारण खारिज किया जा सकता है, विरोधाभासी है।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (a) को खारिज करें: सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने NJAC को स्वीकार नहीं किया — इसे खारिज कर दिया गया; यह विकल्प तथ्यात्मक रूप से गलत है।
विकल्प (b) को खारिज करें: राज्य की स्वीकृति वास्तव में पूरी हो गई थी, लेकिन कोर्ट ने इसे मूल संरचना के प्रश्न से असंबंधित माना — सही प्रक्रिया होने से मौलिक अमान्यता से सुरक्षा नहीं मिलती।
विकल्प (c) को खारिज करें: कानून मंत्री के शामिल होने को समस्या के रूप में देखा गया, लेकिन सटीक निर्णय 'नियुक्तियों में न्यायपालिका की प्रधानता' को मूल संरचना के तत्व के रूप में मानता है।
विकल्प (d) की पुष्टि करें: सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने 99वें संशोधन को इसलिए खारिज किया क्योंकि NJAC ने न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता को प्रभावित किया, जो संविधान की मूल संरचना का हिस्सा है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: NJAC का निर्णय यह दर्शाता है कि प्रक्रिया का पालन — जिसमें राज्य की स्वीकृति भी शामिल है — एक संवैधानिक संशोधन को मूल संरचना की चुनौती से सुरक्षित नहीं रखता। कई छात्र गलत रूप से मानते हैं कि यदि संसद ने सही संशोधन प्रक्रिया (विशेष बहुमत + राज्य की स्वीकृति) का पालन किया है, तो अदालतें संशोधन को अमान्य नहीं कर सकतीं। यह प्रश्न सीधे इस भ्रांति का परीक्षण करता है। सही समझ यह है कि प्रक्रिया की वैधता और सामग्री की वैधता स्वतंत्र आवश्यकताएँ हैं।
hi.final_explanation:
99वां संशोधन (2014) कॉलेजियम प्रणाली की जगह राष्ट्रीय न्यायिक नियुक्ति आयोग (NJAC) लाया — जो 6 सदस्यों वाली संस्था थी, जिसमें भारत के मुख्य न्यायाधीश, दो वरिष्ठ न्यायाधीश, केंद्रीय कानून मंत्री, और दो 'प्रतिष्ठित व्यक्ति' शामिल थे।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: सुप्रीम कोर्ट ने NJAC को स्वीकार नहीं किया — इसे 2015 के निर्णय में 4:1 बहुमत से सर्वसम्मति से खारिज कर दिया गया।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: संशोधन को आधे से अधिक राज्यों ने स्वीकृति दी थी, जो प्रक्रिया की आवश्यकताओं को पूरा करता है। कोर्ट ने कहा कि सही प्रक्रिया होने से ऐसा संशोधन जो मूल संरचना का उल्लंघन करता है, बच नहीं सकता।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: कानून मंत्री के शामिल होने को चिंता का विषय माना गया, लेकिन मुख्य निर्णय व्यापक था — न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता को मूल संरचना का तत्व माना गया।
• विकल्प (d) — सही: कोर्ट ने कहा कि NJAC ने न्यायिक स्वतंत्रता का उल्लंघन किया, जो मूल संरचना का हिस्सा है, इसलिए संशोधन को खारिज कर दिया।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• यह मामला है: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015)।
• न्यायिक नियुक्तियों में 'न्यायपालिका की प्रधानता' को मूल संरचना का तत्व घोषित किया गया।
• कॉलेजियम प्रणाली (जो Three Judges Cases के माध्यम से विकसित हुई) को इस निर्णय द्वारा पुनर्स्थापित किया गया।

shared.concept_anchor: 100th Amendment — enclave exchange numbers and states

en.display_text:
Which of the following pairs related to the 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015 is correctly matched?

(a) India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh : Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India
(b) States whose territorial description was amended : West Bengal and Assam only
(c) India transferred 51 enclaves to Bangladesh : Bangladesh transferred 111 enclaves to India
(d) The foundational international agreement given effect by this amendment : Land Boundary Agreement of 2008
en.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students may recall that the exchange involved Bangladesh and India giving each other different numbers of enclaves, but may swap which side gave more.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Tripura was affected but the amendment covered four states — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura; stating only two affected states is incorrect.
Eliminate option (c): India transferred 111 enclaves TO Bangladesh, not 51. Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India — option (c) reverses the numbers.
Eliminate option (d): The LBA of 1974 was the agreement given effect by this amendment, not an agreement from 2008.
Confirm option (a): India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh, and Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India — these numbers are correctly paired.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The enclave exchange numbers (111 by India, 51 by Bangladesh) are a precision trap. Students who recall the exchange but not the direction or the specific numbers will be drawn to option (c), which reverses the figures. The asymmetry — India gave more than it received — is a notable fact that students often get backwards.
en.final_explanation:
The 100th Amendment (2015) gave constitutional effect to the Land Boundary Agreement of 1974 between India and Bangladesh, under which India and Bangladesh exchanged enclaves — territories of one country surrounded by the other.

• Option (a) — Correct: India transferred 111 enclaves to Bangladesh; Bangladesh transferred 51 enclaves to India. This required amending the First Schedule to reflect the changed territorial descriptions of four states.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Four states were affected — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura — not just two.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This reverses the numbers. India gave 111, Bangladesh gave 51 — not the other way around.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The foundational agreement was signed in 1974, not 2008.

Value Addition:
• The 100th Amendment required state ratification because it altered the First Schedule (territorial descriptions affecting states).
• The four affected states — Assam, West Bengal, Meghalaya, and Tripura — ratified the amendment.
• This was a rare instance where a constitutional amendment directly altered India's international boundaries.

hi.display_text:
100वें संवैधानिक संशोधन अधिनियम, 2015 से संबंधित निम्नलिखित जोड़ों में से कौन-सा सही मेल खाता है?

(a) भारत ने बांग्लादेश को 111 एन्क्लेव स्थानांतरित किए : बांग्लादेश ने भारत को 51 एन्क्लेव स्थानांतरित किए
(b) जिन राज्यों के क्षेत्रीय विवरण में संशोधन किया गया : केवल पश्चिम बंगाल और असम
(c) भारत ने बांग्लादेश को 51 एन्क्लेव स्थानांतरित किए : बांग्लादेश ने भारत को 111 एन्क्लेव स्थानांतरित किए
(d) इस संशोधन द्वारा प्रभाव में लाया गया मौलिक अंतरराष्ट्रीय समझौता : 2008 का भूमि सीमा समझौता
hi.strong_distractor: c — विकल्प (c) भ्रमित करने वाला है क्योंकि छात्र याद कर सकते हैं कि विनिमय में भारत और बांग्लादेश ने एक-दूसरे को अलग-अलग संख्या में एन्क्लेव दिए, लेकिन कौन अधिक दिया, इसे उलट सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (b) को खारिज करें: त्रिपुरा प्रभावित हुआ था लेकिन संशोधन में चार राज्य शामिल थे — असम, पश्चिम बंगाल, मेघालय, और त्रिपुरा; केवल दो प्रभावित राज्यों का उल्लेख करना गलत है।

en.display_text:
With reference to the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 and the Goods and Services Tax framework, consider the following statements:

1. Under Article 279A, GST Council decisions require a three-fourths weighted majority, with the Central Government holding a weightage of one-third of the total votes.
2. The 101st Amendment completely excluded all petroleum products from GST, with no constitutional provision for their future inclusion even through a GST Council recommendation.
3. Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is permanently excluded from GST and can never be brought under its purview through any constitutional mechanism.

Which of the above statements is/are NOT correct?

(a) 1 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 3 only
(d) 1 and 2 only

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 279A, the GST Council requires decisions to be made by a majority of not less than three-fourths of the weighted votes cast, where the Central Government has a weightage of one-third of the total votes.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 279A(9) specifies that decisions require a three-fourths majority of weighted votes; the Centre holds 1/3rd and states collectively hold 2/3rd — correctly stated.

statement_analysis.statement: The 101st Amendment completely excluded all petroleum products from the purview of GST, with no provision for their future inclusion even by the GST Council.
statement_analysis.reason: While petroleum products are currently outside GST, Article 279A(5) allows the GST Council to recommend a date from which petroleum crude, diesel, petrol, natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel shall be brought under GST — future inclusion is constitutionally possible.

statement_analysis.statement: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is permanently excluded from GST and cannot be brought under its purview through a GST Council recommendation.
statement_analysis.reason: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is excluded from GST with no provision in the 101st Amendment for its future inclusion through GST Council recommendation — unlike petroleum products, there is no such enabling clause. However, the statement saying 'permanently' and 'cannot be brought' overstates the constitutional position as it conflates the two categories.

en.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because Statement 3 involves a subtle distinction between alcoholic liquor (absolute exclusion) and petroleum products (conditional exclusion), and students may misidentify either as permanently excluded.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: The 3/4th majority requirement and Centre's 1/3rd weightage are accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct and cannot be the 'NOT correct' answer.

Evaluate Statement 2: The claim that there is 'no provision for future inclusion' is false — Article 279A(5) explicitly allows GST Council to bring petroleum products under GST; Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Evaluate Statement 3: While alcoholic liquor is excluded with no equivalent enabling clause, 'permanently' and 'cannot' overstate the position — the Constitution does not say 'permanently'; Statement 3 is NOT correct as written.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — option (b) is the answer.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The distinction between petroleum products (conditionally excluded — GST Council can recommend inclusion) and alcoholic liquor (excluded without a similar enabling clause) is a high-precision area. Students often remember 'petrol and liquor are outside GST' as a single fact without distinguishing the legal mechanism of exclusion. Statement 2 adds the further trap of 'no provision for future inclusion,' which is directly contradicted by Article 279A(5).
en.final_explanation:
The 101st Amendment (2016) revolutionised India's fiscal federal structure by creating concurrent taxing powers under Article 246A. The GST Council (Article 279A) is the key governance institution.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Three-fourths weighted majority is required; Centre has 1/3rd, states collectively 2/3rd.
• Statement 2 — NOT Correct: Petroleum products are excluded from GST currently, but Article 279A(5) explicitly allows the GST Council to recommend a date for their inclusion — 'no provision for future inclusion' is false.
• Statement 3 — NOT Correct: While alcoholic liquor is excluded without an equivalent inclusion mechanism, describing this as 'permanently cannot be brought' overstates what the Constitution says; and the framing conflates liquor with petroleum products.

Value Addition:
• Five petroleum products currently outside GST: petroleum crude, motor spirit (petrol), high-speed diesel, natural gas, and aviation turbine fuel.
• Tobacco products are within GST but also attract additional Central excise duty.
• The IGST (Integrated GST) applies to inter-state supply of goods and services — managed by the Centre and then apportioned.

shared.concept_anchor: 102nd Amendment NCBC vs 105th Amendment state SEBC power

en.display_text:
Consider the following statements regarding the 102nd and 105th Constitutional Amendment Acts:

Statement 1: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes and introduced Article 342A, which empowers the President to specify Socially and Educationally Backward Classes for the Central list.
Statement 2: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 was enacted to reinforce the 102nd Amendment's position that only the President has the power to identify OBCs, thereby removing any residual power of states in this matter.

Which of the following is correct?

(a) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct
(b) Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are incorrect
(c) Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect
(d) Statement 1 is incorrect but Statement 2 is correct

statement_analysis.statement: The 102nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes and introduced Article 342A, which empowers the President to specify Socially and Educationally Backward Classes.
statement_analysis.reason: The 102nd Amendment inserted Article 338B (NCBC) and Article 342A, which established a Presidential power to specify SEBCs — analogous to the President's power for SCs (Article 341) and STs (Article 342).

statement_analysis.statement: The 105th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2021 was enacted to reinforce the 102nd Amendment's position that only the President has the power to identify OBCs, thereby removing any residual state power in this matter.
statement_analysis.reason: The 105th Amendment was enacted to REVERSE the interpretation that removed state power — specifically to restore states' authority to maintain their own SEBC lists, which had been negated by the Supreme Court's interpretation of Article 342A following the 102nd Amendment (Maratha reservation case).

en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because the 102nd and 105th Amendments are connected, and students may assume the 105th Amendment extended or reinforced the 102nd rather than partially reversed its judicial interpretation.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The 102nd Amendment inserted Articles 338B and 342A — NCBC's constitutional status and Presidential power to specify SEBCs are accurately described; Statement 1 is correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: The 105th Amendment was specifically enacted to restore state power to identify OBCs for their own lists — it reversed the SC's Maratha judgment, not reinforced centralization; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Since Statement 1 is correct and Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The relationship between the 102nd and 105th Amendments is the trap. Students who know both amendments were about OBCs may assume they worked in the same direction — centralising OBC identification. In fact, the 105th Amendment corrected an unintended consequence of the 102nd: after the 102nd Amendment, the Supreme Court held (in the Maratha case) that only the President could notify OBCs, removing state power entirely. The 105th Amendment reversed this to restore state power.
en.final_explanation:
The 102nd and 105th Amendments together tell a story of legislative response to judicial interpretation gone further than intended.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to NCBC under Article 338B and introduced Article 342A, enabling the President to specify SEBCs for the Central list.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The 105th Amendment (2021) was enacted to restore, not reinforce centralization. After the SC interpreted Article 342A as removing state power to identify their own SEBCs, Parliament reversed this through the 105th Amendment — states can maintain their own SEBC lists independently.

Value Addition:
• Pre-102nd Amendment, the NCBC was a statutory body under the NCBC Act, 1993.
• The Maratha reservation case (Indra Sawhney II) was the trigger for the 105th Amendment.
• Article 342A parallels Articles 341 (SCs) and 342 (STs) but is unique in having a state-level parallel list preserved by the 105th Amendment.

shared.concept_anchor: I.R. Coelho — April 24 1973 cutoff for Ninth Schedule immunity

en.display_text:
In the context of the I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) judgment, which of the following statements correctly describes the rule laid down regarding the Ninth Schedule?

(a) All laws placed in the Ninth Schedule, regardless of when they were inserted, enjoy absolute immunity from judicial review under Fundamental Rights
(b) Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution
(c) The cutoff date for Ninth Schedule immunity is January 26, 1950 — laws placed in the Schedule after the Constitution came into force are reviewable
(d) Laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute immunity because they represent Parliament's considered legislative judgment
en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who recall that Kesavananda Bharati (1973) set the Basic Structure doctrine may not remember the precise date — April 24, 1973 — and may instead assume the cutoff operates from the year 1973 generally.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Laws added before April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute protection — not 'complete immunity regardless of date'; absolute immunity applies only to pre-Kesavananda laws.
Eliminate option (c): The cutoff date is April 24, 1973 (date of Kesavananda judgment), not January 26, 1950 (Constitution's commencement date).
Eliminate option (d): Laws added after April 24, 1973 are subject to judicial review for Basic Structure violations — they do not enjoy absolute immunity.
Confirm option (b): The I.R. Coelho judgment established that laws inserted into the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 can be challenged if they violate Basic Structure.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The precise date — April 24, 1973 — is the critical detail. This is the date the Kesavananda Bharati judgment was pronounced, and I.R. Coelho used this as the cutoff for Ninth Schedule immunity. Students who know the year (1973) but not the date may select option (a), which implies a blanket immunity without a date-specific distinction. The date also risks confusion with January 26, 1950 (Constitution's commencement) which appears in option (c) as a plausible-sounding alternative.
en.final_explanation:
The I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) judgment by a 9-judge bench fundamentally changed the understanding of Ninth Schedule immunity.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Absolute immunity is not the universal rule; it applies only to laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
• Option (b) — Correct: Laws added to the Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (the Kesavananda judgment date) are subject to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: January 26, 1950 is the Constitution's commencement date, not the I.R. Coelho cutoff.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Reverses the rule — pre-1973 laws are protected; post-1973 laws are reviewable.

Value Addition:
• The Ninth Schedule grew from 13 laws (1951) to 284 laws, with many added after 1973.
• April 24, 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati pronouncement — a key constitutional calendar date.
• The I.R. Coelho ruling effectively subjects post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to Part III scrutiny filtered through the Basic Structure test.

shared.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — original vs expanded Article 31C

en.display_text:
With reference to the Supreme Court's judgment in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), consider the following statements:

1. The Court struck down the expanded version of Article 31C inserted by the 42nd Amendment, which had given all Directive Principles primacy over all Fundamental Rights.
2. The Court also struck down the original Article 31C inserted by the 25th Amendment, which had protected laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) of the Directive Principles.
3. The judgment declared that a harmonious balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself an element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

(a) 1 and 3 only
(b) 2 and 3 only
(c) 1 only
(d) 1, 2 and 3

statement_analysis.statement: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Supreme Court struck down the expanded version of Article 31C inserted by the 42nd Amendment, which had given all Directive Principles primacy over all Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: The 42nd Amendment had expanded Article 31C to protect laws implementing any DPSP from Fundamental Rights challenges. Minerva Mills struck this down while retaining the original Article 31C (protecting laws under Articles 39(b) and 39(c) only).

statement_analysis.statement: Minerva Mills also struck down the original Article 31C inserted by the 25th Amendment, which protected laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) of the Directive Principles.
statement_analysis.reason: The original Article 31C — protecting laws aimed at achieving Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — was specifically upheld in Minerva Mills; only the expanded version covering all DPSPs was struck down.

statement_analysis.statement: The Minerva Mills judgment declared that the harmonious balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is itself an element of the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: The Court held in Minerva Mills that the balance between Parts III and IV of the Constitution — between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles — is a core element of the Basic Structure that Parliament cannot destroy.

en.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'all three' is tempting because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and may lead students to carelessly accept Statement 2 without recalling the specific distinction between the original and expanded Article 31C.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1: The expanded Article 31C (all DPSPs over all FRs) was struck down in Minerva Mills — correct.
Test Statement 2: The original Article 31C (39(b) and 39(c) only) was UPHELD, not struck down — Statement 2 is incorrect; eliminate options treating it as correct.
Confirm Statement 3: Harmony between FR and DPSP as a Basic Structure element was explicitly declared in Minerva Mills — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — answer is option (a).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The original vs. expanded Article 31C is the precision trap. Both versions of Article 31C are real; only the expanded version was struck down. A student who remembers 'Minerva Mills struck down Article 31C' without distinguishing original from expanded will incorrectly accept Statement 2 as correct, selecting option (d). The two-tier nature of Article 31C's history is a favourite UPSC testing dimension.
en.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills (1980) is the third pillar of the amendment-judicial review trilogy, and its most important contribution was clarifying the limits of parliamentary amendment power and the relationship between Parts III and IV.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The expanded Article 31C (from 42nd Amendment), which gave all DPSPs supremacy over all Fundamental Rights, was struck down as destroying the constitutional balance.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The original Article 31C from the 25th Amendment — protecting laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) — was specifically upheld, not struck down.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Court declared that harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is a Basic Structure element — Parliament cannot tilt the balance entirely in favour of either.

Value Addition:
• Articles 39(b) and 39(c) concern equitable distribution of material resources and prevention of concentration of wealth.
• Minerva Mills also held that limited amending power is a Basic Structure element — Parliament cannot grant itself unlimited amending power.
• The judgment restored the balance that the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment had disrupted.

shared.concept_anchor: 104th Amendment — SC/ST reservation extended, Anglo-Indian seats abolished

en.display_text:
Assertion (A): The 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019 abolished the provision for the nomination of Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies.

Reason (R): The same amendment extended the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies for a further period of ten years.

(a) Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
(c) A is correct but R is incorrect
(d) A is incorrect but R is correct
en.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may correctly recall that the 104th Amendment abolished Anglo-Indian nominated seats and assume the Reason about SC/ST reservation being a separate provision is somehow incorrect.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. The 104th Amendment (2019) abolished nominated Anglo-Indian seats in Lok Sabha (Article 331) and state assemblies (Article 333).

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The 104th Amendment also extended the reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and state assemblies for a further 10 years (2020 to 2030) by amending Article 334.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. The abolition of Anglo-Indian seats and the extension of SC/ST reservation are two independent actions in the same amendment — one did not cause or logically explain the other.
Both A and R are correct but R does not explain A — answer is option (b).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: Students may conflate the two changes made by the 104th Amendment — abolition of Anglo-Indian seats and extension of SC/ST reservation — into a single narrative of 'minority representation changes.' The trap is that R (extension of SC/ST reservation) is factually true but is a separate action with no causal connection to A (abolition of Anglo-Indian seats). Both happened in the same amendment but for entirely independent policy reasons.
en.final_explanation:
The 104th Amendment (2019) made two structurally distinct changes to the Constitution. These changes were both part of the same amending act but arose from completely different policy rationales.

Assertion analysis: Articles 331 and 333, which provided for nomination of Anglo-Indian members to Parliament and state assemblies, were abolished — Assertion is correct.

Reason analysis: Article 334 was amended to extend reservation for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha and state assemblies for another 10 years (until 2030) — Reason is also factually correct.

Causal relationship: R does not explain A. The abolition of Anglo-Indian seats was driven by the community's declining demographic presence; the extension of SC/ST reservation reflects continued socio-economic need. These are independent policy choices — not causally linked.

Value Addition:
• Anglo-Indian nominated seats had been periodically extended since the Constitution came into force — the 104th Amendment ended this practice.
• Article 334 originally set 10 years for SC/ST reservation; it has been extended multiple times through amendment.
• SC/ST reservation in legislatures is for seats, not for nomination — they contest general elections in reserved constituencies.

चरण 3: क्या R, A को कारणात्मक रूप से समझाता है? — नहीं। एंग्लो-इंडियन सीटों का उन्मूलन और अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण का विस्तार एक ही संशोधन में दो स्वतंत्र कार्य हैं — एक ने दूसरे को कारण या तार्किक व्याख्या नहीं दी।
A और R दोनों सही हैं लेकिन R, A को समझाता नहीं है — उत्तर विकल्प (b) है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: छात्र 104वें संशोधन द्वारा किए गए दो परिवर्तनों — एंग्लो-इंडियन सीटों के उन्मूलन और अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण के विस्तार — को 'अल्पसंख्यक प्रतिनिधित्व में परिवर्तन' के एक ही कथानक में मिला सकते हैं। जाल यह है कि R (अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण का विस्तार) तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है लेकिन यह एक अलग कार्य है जिसका A (एंग्लो-इंडियन सीटों का उन्मूलन) से कोई कारणात्मक संबंध नहीं है। दोनों एक ही संशोधन में हुए लेकिन पूरी तरह से स्वतंत्र नीतिगत कारणों से।
hi.final_explanation:
104वां संशोधन (2019) संविधान में दो संरचनात्मक रूप से भिन्न परिवर्तन करता है। ये परिवर्तन एक ही संशोधन अधिनियम का हिस्सा थे लेकिन पूरी तरह से अलग नीतिगत तर्कों से उत्पन्न हुए।

कथन विश्लेषण: अनुच्छेद 331 और 333, जो संसद और राज्य विधानसभाओं में एंग्लो-इंडियन सदस्यों के नामांकन के प्रावधान थे, समाप्त कर दिए गए — कथन सही है।

कारण विश्लेषण: अनुच्छेद 334 में संशोधन किया गया ताकि लोकसभा और राज्य विधानसभाओं में अनुसूचित जाति और जनजाति के लिए आरक्षण को अगले 10 वर्षों (2030 तक) के लिए बढ़ाया जा सके — कारण भी तथ्यात्मक रूप से सही है।

कारणात्मक संबंध: R, A को समझाता नहीं है। एंग्लो-इंडियन सीटों का उन्मूलन समुदाय की घटती जनसांख्यिकीय उपस्थिति के कारण था; अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण का विस्तार सामाजिक-आर्थिक आवश्यकता को दर्शाता है। ये स्वतंत्र नीतिगत विकल्प हैं — कारणात्मक रूप से जुड़े नहीं।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• एंग्लो-इंडियन नामित सीटें संविधान लागू होने के बाद से समय-समय पर बढ़ाई जाती रही हैं — 104वें संशोधन ने इस प्रथा को समाप्त किया।
• अनुच्छेद 334 ने मूल रूप से अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण के लिए 10 वर्ष निर्धारित किए थे; इसे संशोधन के माध्यम से कई बार बढ़ाया गया है।
• विधानसभाओं में अनुसूचित जाति/जनजाति आरक्षण सीटों के लिए है, नामांकन के लिए नहीं — वे आरक्षित निर्वाचन क्षेत्रों में सामान्य चुनाव लड़ते हैं।

shared.concept_anchor: Golak Nath–24th Amendment–Kesavananda–42nd Amendment–Minerva Mills sequence

en.display_text:
Which of the following correctly represents the chronological interleaving of landmark Supreme Court judgments and constitutional amendments in the evolution of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution?

(a) Kesavananda Bharati → 24th Amendment → Golak Nath → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills
(b) Golak Nath → Kesavananda Bharati → 24th Amendment → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills
(c) Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda Bharati → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills
(d) 24th Amendment → Golak Nath → 42nd Amendment → Kesavananda Bharati → Minerva Mills
en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because students who know the broad sequence (Golak Nath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills) may forget that the 24th Amendment came between Golak Nath and Kesavananda, and place the 42nd Amendment incorrectly.
elimination_logic: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab was decided in 1967 — it comes first in the sequence.
The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's response to Golak Nath — it comes after Golak Nath but before Kesavananda.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) responded to the 24th Amendment — it comes next, establishing Basic Structure.

The 42nd Amendment (1976) was Parliament's response to Kesavananda — it comes after; then Minerva Mills (1980) responded to the 42nd Amendment. Correct sequence: Golak Nath → 24th Amendment → Kesavananda → 42nd Amendment → Minerva Mills = option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap lies in the interleaved sequence of judicial decisions and constitutional amendments. Students who study judicial cases and constitutional amendments in separate silos know the sequence within each category but may fail to correctly interleave them. The most common error is placing the 42nd Amendment before Kesavananda (wrong — the 42nd Amendment was a response to Kesavananda) or placing the 24th Amendment after Kesavananda.
en.final_explanation:
The Golak Nath–Kesavananda–Minerva Mills trilogy is not purely judicial — it is a back-and-forth between Parliament (through amendments) and the judiciary (through judgments). Understanding the interleaved sequence is essential.

Correct sequence:
1. Golak Nath (1967): FR cannot be amended at all.
2. 24th Amendment (1971): Parliament's response — FR can be amended; Article 13 and 368 modified.
3. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): FR can be amended but Basic Structure cannot be destroyed.
4. 42nd Amendment (1976): Parliament's response — attempted to grant itself unlimited amending power (struck down later).
5. Minerva Mills (1980): Supreme Court's response — struck down the 42nd Amendment's Clauses 4 and 5; limited amending power is itself a Basic Structure element.

Why other options fail: Options (a), (b), and (d) incorrectly interleave the judicial and legislative responses.

Value Addition:
• Each amendment was a direct parliamentary retaliation against the preceding judicial decision.
• The 25th Amendment (1971) was also part of this period — it inserted Article 31C.
• Prospective overruling was applied for the first time in Indian law in Golak Nath.

hi.display_text:
संसद की संविधान संशोधन शक्ति के विकास में सुप्रीम कोर्ट के महत्वपूर्ण निर्णयों और संवैधानिक संशोधनों के कालानुक्रमिक अंतःस्थापन का सही क्रम कौन-सा है?

(a) Kesavananda Bharati → 24वां संशोधन → Golak Nath → 42वां संशोधन → Minerva Mills
(b) Golak Nath → Kesavananda Bharati → 24वां संशोधन → 42वां संशोधन → Minerva Mills
(c) Golak Nath → 24वां संशोधन → Kesavananda Bharati → 42वां संशोधन → Minerva Mills
(d) 24वां संशोधन → Golak Nath → 42वां संशोधन → Kesavananda Bharati → Minerva Mills
hi.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प (b) एक मजबूत भ्रम है क्योंकि जो छात्र व्यापक अनुक्रम (Golak Nath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills) जानते हैं, वे भूल सकते हैं कि 24वां संशोधन Golak Nath और Kesavananda के बीच आया था, और 42वें संशोधन को गलत स्थान पर रख देते हैं।
elimination_logic: Golak Nath v. State of Punjab 1967 में निर्णय हुआ था — यह अनुक्रम में सबसे पहले आता है।
24वां संशोधन (1971) संसद की Golak Nath के प्रति प्रतिक्रिया थी — यह Golak Nath के बाद लेकिन Kesavananda से पहले आता है।
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) 24वें संशोधन के प्रति प्रतिक्रिया थी — यह अगला आता है, जिसने मूल संरचना (Basic Structure) स्थापित की।

42वां संशोधन (1976) संसद की Kesavananda के प्रति प्रतिक्रिया थी — यह बाद में आता है; फिर Minerva Mills (1980) 42वें संशोधन के प्रति प्रतिक्रिया थी। सही अनुक्रम: Golak Nath → 24वां संशोधन → Kesavananda → 42वां संशोधन → Minerva Mills = विकल्प (c)।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: फंदा न्यायिक निर्णयों और संवैधानिक संशोधनों के अंतःस्थापित अनुक्रम में है। जो छात्र न्यायिक मामलों और संवैधानिक संशोधनों को अलग-अलग अध्ययन करते हैं, वे प्रत्येक श्रेणी के भीतर अनुक्रम जानते हैं लेकिन उन्हें सही ढंग से अंतःस्थापित करने में विफल हो सकते हैं। सबसे आम त्रुटि 42वें संशोधन को Kesavananda से पहले रखना है (गलत — 42वां संशोधन Kesavananda के प्रति प्रतिक्रिया था) या 24वें संशोधन को Kesavananda के बाद रखना।
hi.final_explanation:
Golak Nath–Kesavananda–Minerva Mills त्रयी केवल न्यायिक नहीं है — यह संसद (संशोधनों के माध्यम से) और न्यायपालिका (निर्णयों के माध्यम से) के बीच एक परस्पर प्रतिक्रिया है। अंतःस्थापित अनुक्रम को समझना आवश्यक है।

सही अनुक्रम:
1. Golak Nath (1967): मौलिक अधिकारों को संशोधित नहीं किया जा सकता।
2. 24वां संशोधन (1971): संसद की प्रतिक्रिया — मौलिक अधिकारों को संशोधित किया जा सकता है; अनुच्छेद 13 और 368 में संशोधन।
3. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): मौलिक अधिकारों को संशोधित किया जा सकता है लेकिन मूल संरचना को नष्ट नहीं किया जा सकता।
4. 42वां संशोधन (1976): संसद की प्रतिक्रिया — स्वयं को असीम संशोधन शक्ति देने का प्रयास (बाद में खारिज)।
5. Minerva Mills (1980): सर्वोच्च न्यायालय की प्रतिक्रिया — 42वें संशोधन के खंड 4 और 5 को खारिज किया; सीमित संशोधन शक्ति स्वयं मूल संरचना का तत्व है।

अन्य विकल्प क्यों गलत हैं: विकल्प (a), (b), और (d) न्यायिक और विधायी प्रतिक्रियाओं को गलत ढंग से अंतःस्थापित करते हैं।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• प्रत्येक संशोधन पूर्ववर्ती न्यायिक निर्णय के प्रति प्रत्यक्ष संसदीय प्रतिक्रिया था।
• 25वां संशोधन (1971) भी इस अवधि का हिस्सा था — इसने अनुच्छेद 31C जोड़ा।
• भारतीय कानून में पहली बार Golak Nath में prospective overruling लागू किया गया।

table_data.header_text: Match the constitutional changes in List I with the amendment that introduced them in List II:
rows: A. Addition of the words 'Socialist', 'Secular', and 'Integrity' to the Preamble
1. 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — Fundamental Duties
B. Restoration of the original five-year term for the Lok Sabha
2. 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 — Preamble
C. Removal of the Right to Property from the list of Fundamental Rights
3. 44th Amendment Act, 1978 — Right to Property
D. Addition of Fundamental Duties under a new Part IVA (Article 51A)
4. 44th Amendment Act, 1978 — Lok Sabha term
table_data.footer_text:
Which of the following is the correct matching?

(a) A-1, B-4, C-3, D-2
(b) A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1
(c) A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1
(d) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4

en.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students who know the 42nd Amendment added Fundamental Duties and the 44th Amendment restored the 5-year term may correctly place A and B but then swap C and D.
elimination_logic: A (Words 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' added to Preamble) → 42nd Amendment (1976); matches List II item 2.
B (Restoration of 5-year term for Lok Sabha) → 44th Amendment (1978); matches List II item 4.
C (Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights) → 44th Amendment (1978); matches List II item 3.
D (Addition of Fundamental Duties under Part IVA) → 42nd Amendment (1976); matches List II item 1. Correct: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 = option (c).
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap operates between the 42nd and 44th Amendments, which are closely related in the Emergency and post-Emergency period. Students know both are important but may attribute features of one to the other. Specifically, the Right to Property deletion (44th Amendment) and the addition of Fundamental Duties (42nd Amendment) are commonly confused in attribution.
en.final_explanation:
The 42nd and 44th Amendments bracket the Emergency period — the former enacted during Emergency (1976), the latter as a corrective after (1978).

• A (Words 'Socialist', 'Secular', 'Integrity' in Preamble) → 42nd Amendment (1976). These words reflected the ideological framing of the Emergency era.
• B (Restoration of 5-year Lok Sabha term) → 44th Amendment (1978). The 42nd had extended terms to 6 years; the 44th reversed this.
• C (Right to Property removed from Fundamental Rights) → 44th Amendment (1978). Property became a legal right under Article 300A.
• D (Fundamental Duties added, Part IVA, Article 51A) → 42nd Amendment (1976). Originally 10 duties were added.

Correct matching: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1.

Value Addition:
• The 11th Fundamental Duty was added by the 86th Amendment (2002): duty to provide education opportunities to children.
• The 42nd Amendment also extended Lok Sabha and state assembly terms from 5 to 6 years (reversed by 44th).
• Articles 20 and 21 were declared non-suspendable even during Emergency by the 44th Amendment.

rows: A. प्रस्तावना में 'समाजवादी', 'धार्मिक निरपेक्षता' और 'अखंडता' शब्दों का जोड़
1. 42वां संशोधन अधिनियम, 1976 — मौलिक कर्तव्य
B. लोकसभा के मूल पांच-वर्षीय कार्यकाल की पुनर्स्थापना
2. 42वां संशोधन अधिनियम, 1976 — प्रस्तावना
C. मौलिक अधिकारों से संपत्ति के अधिकार को हटाना
3. 44वां संशोधन अधिनियम, 1978 — संपत्ति का अधिकार
D. भाग IVA (अनुच्छेद 51A) के तहत मौलिक कर्तव्यों का जोड़
4. 44वां संशोधन अधिनियम, 1978 — लोकसभा कार्यकाल

hi.strong_distractor: a — विकल्प (a) एक मजबूत भ्रम पैदा करने वाला है क्योंकि जो छात्र जानते हैं कि 42वें संशोधन ने मौलिक कर्तव्य जोड़े और 44वें संशोधन ने 5-वर्षीय कार्यकाल बहाल किया, वे सही रूप से A और B को रख सकते हैं लेकिन फिर C और D को उलट देते हैं।
elimination_logic: A (संविधान के प्रस्तावना में 'समाजवादी', 'धार्मिक निरपेक्षता', 'अखंडता' शब्द जोड़े गए) → 42वां संशोधन (1976); सूची II के आइटम 2 से मेल खाता है।
B (लोकसभा के मूल 5-वर्षीय कार्यकाल की पुनर्स्थापना) → 44वां संशोधन (1978); सूची II के आइटम 4 से मेल खाता है।
C (मौलिक अधिकारों से संपत्ति के अधिकार को हटाना) → 44वां संशोधन (1978); सूची II के आइटम 3 से मेल खाता है।
D (मौलिक कर्तव्यों का भाग IVA के तहत जोड़ना) → 42वां संशोधन (1976); सूची II के आइटम 1 से मेल खाता है। सही: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1 = विकल्प (c)।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: 42वें और 44वें संशोधनों के बीच वस्तु-स्थानांतरण होता है, जो आपातकाल और आपातकालोत्तर अवधि में निकटता से संबंधित हैं। छात्र दोनों को महत्वपूर्ण जानते हैं लेकिन एक के गुण दूसरे को दे सकते हैं। विशेष रूप से, संपत्ति के अधिकार को हटाना (44वां संशोधन) और मौलिक कर्तव्यों का जोड़ना (42वां संशोधन) आमतौर पर भ्रमित होते हैं।
hi.final_explanation:
42वां और 44वां संशोधन आपातकालीन अवधि को घेरे हुए हैं — पहला आपातकाल के दौरान (1976) लागू हुआ, दूसरा उसके बाद सुधार के रूप में (1978)।

• A (प्रस्तावना में 'समाजवादी', 'धार्मिक निरपेक्षता', 'अखंडता' शब्द) → 42वां संशोधन (1976)। ये शब्द आपातकालीन युग की वैचारिक रूपरेखा को दर्शाते हैं।
• B (लोकसभा के 5-वर्षीय कार्यकाल की पुनर्स्थापना) → 44वां संशोधन (1978)। 42वें ने कार्यकाल 6 वर्ष कर दिया था; 44वें ने इसे वापस किया।
• C (मौलिक अधिकारों से संपत्ति के अधिकार को हटाना) → 44वां संशोधन (1978)। संपत्ति अब अनुच्छेद 300A के तहत कानूनी अधिकार बन गई।
• D (मौलिक कर्तव्य जोड़े गए, भाग IVA, अनुच्छेद 51A) → 42वां संशोधन (1976)। मूल रूप से 10 कर्तव्य जोड़े गए थे।

सही मिलान: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1।

मूल्य संवर्धन:
• 11वां मौलिक कर्तव्य 86वें संशोधन (2002) द्वारा जोड़ा गया: बच्चों को शिक्षा के अवसर प्रदान करना।

shared.concept_anchor: 91st Amendment — cabinet size 15% of Lok Sabha strength

en.display_text:
Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003, provides that the total number of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Council of Ministers shall not exceed ________ of the total strength of the House of the People.

(a) 20 per cent
(b) 10 per cent
(c) 25 per cent
(d) 15 per cent
en.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because 10% appears in constitutional contexts (quorum under Article 100) and students who recall 'a percentage of Lok Sabha' may default to 10 without verifying the precise figure.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): 20% of Lok Sabha strength (543 seats) would mean 108 ministers — this would be an extremely large cabinet and is not the constitutional provision.
Eliminate option (b): 10% is the quorum requirement under Article 100, not the cabinet size cap — a different constitutional number.
Eliminate option (c): 25% would allow 135+ ministers and is not the cap prescribed in Article 75(1A).
Confirm option (d): Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment, caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
en.upsc_trap_explanation: The 15% figure is a precision trap. Constitutional percentages cluster in a student's memory — 10% (quorum), 1/3 and 2/3 (defection), 3/4 (GST Council). The 15% cabinet cap is a specific statutory ceiling that is easy to confuse with 10% or 20% without precise recall. The minimum of 12 for state councils is an additional detail that further tests precision.
en.final_explanation:
The 91st Amendment (2003) introduced a constitutional ceiling on the size of the Council of Ministers to prevent the practice of distributing cabinet berths for political management rather than governance efficiency.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: 20% of Lok Sabha strength is not the constitutional cap.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: 10% is the quorum requirement in Parliament under Article 100 — a different constitutional provision.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: 25% is not the prescribed limit.
• Option (d) — Correct: Article 75(1A) caps the Union Council of Ministers at 15% of the total membership of the Lok Sabha. For state councils, the minimum is 12 ministers and the ceiling is 15% of the state assembly's strength.

Value Addition:
• At Lok Sabha strength of 543, the maximum Union cabinet size is approximately 81 ministers.
• The 15% cap applies separately to each state — states cannot pool limits.
• The 91st Amendment simultaneously raised the merger threshold in the Tenth Schedule from 1/3 to 2/3.

hi.display_text:
91वें संवैधानिक संशोधन अधिनियम, 2003 द्वारा जोड़ा गया अनुच्छेद 75(1A) यह प्रावधान करता है कि मंत्रिपरिषद में प्रधानमंत्री सहित कुल मंत्रियों की संख्या लोकसभा की कुल संख्या के ________ से अधिक नहीं होगी।

(a) 20 प्रतिशत
(b) 10 प्रतिशत
(c) 25 प्रतिशत
(d) 15 प्रतिशत
hi.strong_distractor: b — विकल्प (b) एक मजबूत भ्रम है क्योंकि 10% संवैधानिक संदर्भों (अनुच्छेद 100 के तहत कोरम) में आता है और छात्र जो 'लोकसभा का प्रतिशत' याद करते हैं, वे बिना सटीक आंकड़ा जांचे 10% को चुन सकते हैं।
elimination_logic: विकल्प (a) को हटाएं: लोकसभा की संख्या का 20% (543 सीटें) मतलब 108 मंत्री होंगे — यह अत्यंत बड़ा कैबिनेट होगा और यह संवैधानिक प्रावधान नहीं है।
विकल्प (b) को हटाएं: 10% अनुच्छेद 100 के तहत कोरम की आवश्यकता है, कैबिनेट आकार की सीमा नहीं — यह एक अलग संवैधानिक संख्या है।
विकल्प (c) को हटाएं: 25% से 135+ मंत्री होंगे और यह अनुच्छेद 75(1A) में निर्धारित सीमा नहीं है।
विकल्प (d) की पुष्टि करें: 91वें संशोधन द्वारा जोड़ा गया अनुच्छेद 75(1A) लोकसभा की कुल संख्या के 15% पर मंत्रिपरिषद के आकार को सीमित करता है।
hi.upsc_trap_explanation: 15% का आंकड़ा एक सटीकता जाल है। संवैधानिक प्रतिशत छात्र की स्मृति में समूहित होते हैं — 10% (कोरम), 1/3 और 2/3 (पद छोड़ना), 3/4 (GST परिषद)। 15% कैबिनेट सीमा एक विशिष्ट वैधानिक सीमा है जिसे बिना सटीक स्मृति के 10% या 20% से भ्रमित किया जा सकता है। राज्य परिषदों के लिए न्यूनतम 12 मंत्रियों का विवरण अतिरिक्त जाँच है।
hi.final_explanation:
91वां संशोधन (2003) मंत्रिपरिषद के आकार पर संवैधानिक सीमा प्रस्तुत करता है ताकि राजनीतिक प्रबंधन के लिए कैबिनेट पदों का वितरण करने की प्रथा को रोका जा सके, न कि शासन दक्षता के लिए।

• विकल्प (a) — गलत: लोकसभा की संख्या का 20% संवैधानिक सीमा नहीं है।
• विकल्प (b) — गलत: 10% संसद में अनुच्छेद 100 के तहत कोरम की आवश्यकता है — एक अलग संवैधानिक प्रावधान।
• विकल्प (c) — गलत: 25% निर्धारित सीमा नहीं है।
• विकल्प (d) — सही: अनुच्छेद 75(1A) संघ मंत्रिपरिषद के आकार को लोकसभा की कुल सदस्यता के 15% तक सीमित करता है। राज्य परिषदों के लिए न्यूनतम 12 मंत्री और अधिकतम राज्य विधानसभा की संख्या का 15% है।

मूल्यवर्धन:
• लोकसभा की संख्या 543 होने पर, अधिकतम संघ कैबिनेट आकार लगभग 81 मंत्री होगा।
• 15% सीमा प्रत्येक राज्य पर अलग-अलग लागू होती है — राज्यों को सीमाएँ साझा नहीं करनी हैं।
• 91वें संशोधन ने दसवें अनुसूची में विलय की सीमा को 1/3 से बढ़ाकर 2/3 कर दिया।
